The Small-World Experiment. In 1967, Stanley Milgram conducted a different kind of experiment that would reshape how we think about social networks. He asked people to send letters to a distant stranger by passing them only through acquaintances they knew by first name. The results suggested that vast social networks are connected by surprisingly short chains—the origin of the famous phrase "six degrees of separation."

Milgram gave letters to residents of Kansas and Nebraska addressed to a stockbroker in Boston whom the senders did not know. Each person could only pass the letter to someone they knew personally, writing instructions on the envelope. About sixty-four letters were sent, and roughly one-third completed the chain, reaching the target in an average of five and a half steps.

What struck Milgram most was the structure of these paths. The intermediate nodes were often "funnels"—a small number of well-connected people through whom many chains passed. These connectors were usually determined by geography or profession. Some people acted as bridges between social worlds. The experiment revealed that social networks contain many short paths between any two people, making the world small relative to its size.

Participants showed systematic bias in how they chose intermediaries. They selected people closer in geography and social status to the target, suggesting that people carry mental maps of network structure. They relied on heuristic guessing—pass it to someone in Boston, pass it to someone in finance—rather than knowing actual network paths. The "six degrees of separation" phrase, though not Milgram's own, became a cultural meme, influencing network science, the Kevin Bacon game, and eventually social media itself.
